title: Montaigne travels
hookLine: Montaigne loved travel for the new and the different (Essays 3.9)

lines: UGLY ON THE RIGHT? GO LEFT.
cards: A traveler stands at a fork in the road. On the right, the way looks ugly, so he takes the left. That's the whole plan.
No route marked, no list of sights, no deadline. If he gets somewhere he doesn't like, he leaves; if he forgot to see something, he goes back.
This is Montaigne on the road, in a long, wandering essay of book three called Of vanity. The man who retreated to a tower full of books also loved to leave it.

teach.b: First, the plan that isn't one. He isn't chasing a destination, so he can't be late for it. The road itself is the point.
Second, the new and the different.
Travel, he says, is good exercise for the mind, kept busy noticing what it hasn't seen before.
Other people's ways of eating, dressing and greeting show him the wide variety of human lives, and loosen the grip of his own habits. Third, the travelers he laughs at.

teach.h: DON'T GO ABROAD TO FIND HOME.
teach.b: He pokes fun at people who go abroad only to find their own countrymen, eat their own food and complain about everything foreign. That misses the point of going.
He would rather sit at a stranger's table and eat what they eat. Fourth, the honest answer. People ask what he's looking for on these trips.

teach.h: I KNOW WHAT I FLEE, NOT WHAT I SEEK.
teach.b: He answers, more or less, that he knows well what he's fleeing, but not what he's seeking. It's a strangely freeing confession: not every journey needs a goal written down before it begins.
Sometimes it's enough to need a change of air and trust the road to show you something. None of this needs a plane. A different street to the store, a neighborhood you always drive past.
The mind wakes up a little when it meets something it didn't expect.

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of vanity often take from it his love of unplanned travel, his curiosity about other people's customs, and his line about knowing what he flees but not what he seeks.

games.q: Montaigne on the road: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne planned every leg of his journeys in advance
he describes travel without a fixed route: if the way looks bad on the right, he goes left.
he says he knows what he flees but not what he seeks
his honest answer when people ask what he's looking for.
he admired travelers who stayed among their own countrymen abroad
he pokes fun at them; he'd rather eat at a stranger's table.

games.q: you're on the road with Montaigne and the way ahead looks ugly. what does he do?
o: push on; the plan is the plan.
games.why: if it looks bad on the right, he goes left. there's no fixed route to be late for.

practice: Picture a trip you make most days, to work, the store or the mailbox, and then one small change: a different turn, a different street, a different door.
Don't pick a destination, just the turn, and let your mind wander down that street, curious. If it drifts back to the usual road, take the left again.

wordCard.voice: Montaigne travels. No fixed route, a stranger's table, and a mind kept awake by the new. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a new route. Knowing what you're leaving can be enough to set out. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays 3.9, Of vanity (travel without a fixed route; travel as exercise for the mind among new things; travelers who keep only to their countrymen; I know what I flee, not what I seek)
